title: How much margin relief can a clearing member count on in stress?
summary: The Bank of England’s near-final supervisory statement explains how it expects central counterparties to limit destabilising jumps in initial margin while retaining sufficient collateral to cover a member default. That balance matters to a portfolio manager clearing a hedged position. A hedge can reduce the loss on the combined trade, but the clearing house may recognise only part of the estimated reduction in risk. Even a well-hedged position can generate a substantial cash requirement as volatility rises. The statement describes supervisory expectations and the corresponding proposed rulebook provisions. It gives no estimate of the collateral a particular member would be asked to post.

Figure 1 sets out three competing objectives. Initial margin protects the clearing house and surviving members against losses that might occur before a defaulter’s position can be closed. A model that responds quickly to volatility can provide that protection, but may call for large amounts of collateral just as funding becomes scarce. Keeping more margin throughout calm periods can smooth the increase in a crisis while raising the average cost of clearing. The Bank expects the clearing house to evaluate all three effects for the products it clears and its membership. A model that produces fewer large calls could still be undesirable if it leaves the default fund exposed.

Paragraph 3.10 sets out alternative ways to address this problem. One is a buffer of at least 25% of unadjusted regulatory initial margin, apart from specified non-market-risk add-ons, which can be temporarily drawn down when the underlying margin is rising substantially. Another is a weight of at least 25% on stressed observations in the lookback period. A third puts a floor under margin based on a ten-year volatility lookback. These percentages govern different calculations. At least one anti-procyclicality measure should address each material risk factor capable of creating a large step change. A CCP using the buffer should specify the triggers, approval and replenishment arrangements. It should monitor performance against its tolerance daily, review breaches alongside coverage and cost, and govern any exceptional override.

The portfolio calculation is particularly consequential for relative-value positions. Across different instruments, eligible offsets generally cannot exceed 80% of the difference between their total standalone margin and the combined estimate. Applying that percentage to the entire margin bill would substantially misstate the protection. The Bank distinguishes, for example, rate derivatives in different currencies from otherwise comparable swaps in the same currency with different maturities. Even eligibility for classification as the same product does not by itself justify the maximum reduction. Paragraphs 4.27–4.29 require an underlying economic relationship that imposes an absolute bound on losses for offsets above the ordinary cap. A strong historical correlation alone does not establish that bound.

Section 5 calls for a secure simulator covering actual and hypothetical portfolios under a range of stresses, including important historical episodes and material standard add-ons. Its estimates are indicative, and portfolio-level non-market-risk add-ons are excluded from the specified calculation. Section 6 also distinguishes continuous monitoring of relevant intraday risk indicators from constantly recalculating every margin amount. A desk can use simulated calls to size a liquidity buffer, but the final call still depends on the CCP’s risk assessment, the scope of modelled components and the portfolio on the day.

questions.question: Which positions dominate our largest collateral call after offsets are capped?
questions.detail: The statement explains the 80% calculation and gives examples by asset class. It does not report the effect on any actual portfolio. A manager holding a swap against bond futures needs to know whether reducing gross size or changing the hedge would release more liquidity. Run the CCP’s secure simulator for the combined portfolio and the standalone legs under identical stress inputs, then reconcile the implied offset with the CCP’s own margin methodology.

questions.question: How quickly would an exhausted anti-procyclicality buffer need to be rebuilt?
questions.detail: Paragraph 3.14 requires documented depletion and replenishment arrangements but leaves the calibration to the clearing house. Rebuilding the buffer while funding markets are still tight could create a second call even if price volatility is subsiding. Review the CCP’s published high-level policy and obtain member guidance on triggers and timing. Compare illustrative paths with past calls or a stress simulation spanning the recovery period.

questions.question: How large could the difference be between simulated margin and cash actually due?
questions.detail: The simulator must incorporate important model components but produces a non-binding estimate and excludes specified portfolio-level add-ons. A desk with concentrated exposures may need a larger readily available collateral pool. Seek the CCP’s inventory of included charges, member-specific add-on policies and model-override governance. Compare simulator output with realised calls on representative portfolios during earlier volatile sessions, keeping the portfolio, valuation time and scope of each figure consistent.

limitation: This is a near-final supervisory statement. Its examples describe margin mechanics and potential liquidity needs. They provide no member-level exposures, actual calls or implementation cost estimates.
